subject: Question about kmeans demo for rmr2: how does < key val > pairs get mapped by to.dfs()

messages.author: 7077bbc3ea5cb2cb
messages.subject: Question about kmeans demo for rmr2: how does < key val > pairs get mapped by to.dfs()
parts:
Hi, RHadoop Group,

I'm new to RHadoop and has been palying around the kmeans example for days.

I saw two differnt implementations online, one is on the RHadoop wiki: Comparison-of-high-level-languages-for-mapreduce-k-means, as pasted below

kmeans =
  function(points, ncenters, iterations = 10, distfun = NULL) {
    if(is.null(distfun)) 
      distfun = 
        function(a,b) norm(as.matrix(a-b), type = 'F')
    newCenters = 
      kmeans.iter(
        points, 
        distfun,
        ncenters = ncenters)
    for(i in 1:iterations) {
      newCenters = kmeans.iter(points, distfun, centers = newCenters)}
    newCenters}

kmeans.iter =
  function(points, distfun, ncenters = dim(centers)[1], centers = NULL) {
    from.dfs(mapreduce(input = points,
                         map = 
                           if (is.null(centers)) {
                             function(k,v) keyval(sample(1:ncenters,1),v)} # I'm thinking here v should be a vector, not entire matrix, which means I should not directly use entire matrix as input.
                           else {
                             function(k,v) {
                               distances = apply(centers, 1, function(c) distfun(c,v))
                               keyval(centers[which.min(distances),], v)}},
                         reduce = function(k,vv) keyval(NULL, apply(do.call(rbind, vv), 2, mean))),
             to.data.frame = T)}

It mainly gives me two problems:
1. Error in from.dfs(mapreduce(input = points, map = if (is.null(centers)) { :
  unused argument (to.data.frame = T)
By commenting this option, this error disappear.
2. Error in apply(centers, 1, function(c) distfun(c, v)) :
  dim(X) must have a positive length

The input I was using is to.dfs(small.data)
> str(small.data)
'data.frame':    4 obs. of  8 variables:
 $ x1: num  0.58 0.43 0.64 0.58
 $ x2: num  0.61 0.67 0.62 0.44
 $ x3: num  0.47 0.48 0.49 0.57
 $ x4: num  0.13 0.27 0.15 0.13
 $ x5: num  0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5
 $ x6: num  0 0 0 0
 $ x7: num  0.48 0.53 0.53 0.54
 $ x8: num  0.22 0.22 0.22 0.22

I noticed that after the first round MR (by running kmeans.iter(to.dfs(small.data),distfun,2,center=NULL) ), the center becomes:
$key
NULL

$val
[1] 0.37375 0.38750 0.39375 0.37250

which is not in the correct format. The center should be a 2*8 matrix instead of a vector of 4.

When I tried exactly the same input with another kmeans example on rmr2 tutorial, it works totally fine.

I'm thinking the difference between these two is that, on wiki example, value should be a vector, while on tutorial example, value should be entire matrix. But I don't know how to map data.frame to list of vectors. How exactly does to.dfs() map input to <key,val> pairs?

The other question bothering me is about the performance. In the tutorial kmeans, the mapper is the part parallelization and speed up happens. But is it because when my input data is big, it got splited and hence multiple mappers are created to do the calculation, or is it because within each mapper, the calculation of distance matrix is parallelized over multiple threads, say center 1 to all points, center 2 to all points are different thread?

My intension of using RHadoop is to apply very complex and time-consuming mathematical calculations and statistical analysis on a relatively small data set. I think RHadoop is the one I'm looking for. Just have to learn more about it.

I would highly appreciate any feedbacks. Thanks in advance.

Sincerely,
Lishu

messages.author: 63023c771a070260
messages.subject: Re: Question about kmeans demo for rmr2: how does < key val > pairs get mapped by to.dfs()
parts:
The difference is that the article in the RHadoop wiki is out of date. The rmr2 tutorial is based on code that is tested with every build, included into the tutorial without cut and paste but directly by include. So hopefully that will never go out of date. I am torn between upgrading also the comparison or not, because it's unfair to upgrade only one side of the comparison. I should probably add a note though that to run with the current rmr2 one needs a different version. There is no multithreading, only multiple processes. Applying Hadoop to a small data set is not the typical use case and you may find yourself running into problems, such as insufficient level of parallelism and timeouts being exceeded. But it can be done, for instance there is a famous example of hadoop used to compute an approximation of pi, a job that has almost no input (a number of digits). You can check it out here 

https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/current/api/org/apache/hadoop/examples/pi/package-summary.html

It's in java, not in R, but may be the best match for the application you are thinking about. If you would like to report here about the progress you make, I think it would be valuable.



Antonio
